title: Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma: From Past to Future—A Comprehensive Review of Pathophysiology and Therapeutic Advances

subsections.subsection_title: Historical Discovery and Evolution of Classification
subsections.content:
The historical foundation of Hodgkin lymphoma was laid in 1832 by Thomas Hodgkin, whose seminal paper 'On some Morbid Appearances of the Absorbent Glands and Spleen' first documented distinctive pathological changes in lymphatic tissues, though he did not recognize the characteristic neoplastic cells ref [1]. The disease was later named 'Hodgkin's disease' by Samuel Wilks in 1865, who expanded on Hodgkin’s observations and distinguished it from other lymphatic disorders ref [14]. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Virchow helped differentiate Hodgkin's disease from leukemia, while Sternberg and, more definitively, Dorothy Reed described the hallmark multinucleated Reed–Sternberg cells, establishing the morphological basis for diagnosis ref [14]. The 20th century saw the development of the Ann Arbor staging system in the 1970s, which standardized clinical assessment and treatment stratification based on anatomical spread ref [16]. This system was refined in 1989 at the Cotswolds meeting, where imaging criteria were updated to incorporate CT scans, bulky disease was formally designated with the 'X' suffix, and splenic involvement criteria were clarified to improve global applicability ref [16], ref [18].

The modern classification of Hodgkin lymphoma emerged with the Revised European-American Lymphoma (REAL) classification and was formalized by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2001 and updated in 2017, which bifurcated the disease into two distinct entities: classic Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) and nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma (NLPHL) ref [5]. cHL was further subdivided into four histologic subtypes, while NLPHL was recognized for its unique immunophenotype and morphological patterns, necessitating careful differential diagnosis from other lymphomas ref [5]. The 2008 International Lymphoma Study Group proposal introduced provisional entities such as ALCL, Hodgkin-like, highlighting the evolving molecular distinctions between Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas ref [2]. These classifications reflect a paradigm shift from purely morphological to integrated histopathological, immunophenotypic, and molecular criteria, enhancing diagnostic precision and therapeutic targeting.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (CHL) arises from a complex interplay of genetic, infectious, and environmental factors. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a well-established etiological agent, detected in approximately one-third of CHL cases, with clonal viral DNA present in Reed-Sternberg cells, suggesting infection precedes malignant transformation ref [8]. EBV-associated CHL shows distinct epidemiological patterns, including higher prevalence in mixed cellularity histology and among Hispanic populations, and is strongly linked to prior infectious mononucleosis, particularly in young adults ref [7]. Beyond viral triggers, familial aggregation plays a significant role: first-degree relatives of CHL patients have a threefold increased risk, with siblings facing a sixfold higher risk and monozygotic twins exhibiting up to a 57-fold elevation ref [11]. Perinatal factors, notably high fetal growth, are independently associated with increased CHL risk in childhood and young adulthood, implicating in utero growth factor pathways ref [10]. Genetic susceptibility is further supported by associations with specific single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and a documented family history of cancer, particularly in pediatric and adolescent populations ref [7].

Environmental and lifestyle influences also modulate risk, with smoking and reduced physical activity potentially altering immune surveillance and chronic inflammation, though evidence remains less consistent ref [7]. Geographic and racial disparities in CHL incidence—such as higher childhood prevalence in Asia and the Middle East versus bimodal peaks in Western nations—underscore the role of population-specific gene-environment interactions ref [7]. The convergence of EBV infection, inherited predisposition, and early-life exposures suggests a multifactorial model in which immune dysregulation during critical developmental windows may initiate lymphomagenesis, particularly in genetically susceptible individuals ref [8].

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) originates from crippled germinal center B cells that have undergone somatic hypermutation but lost the ability to express a functional B-cell receptor (BCR) due to destructive mutations in immunoglobulin genes, rendering them unable to transmit survival signals through the BCR. These transformed cells, known as Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells, retain clonal immunoglobulin gene rearrangements, confirming their B-cell lineage in the vast majority of cases, though rare instances of T-cell origin have been documented. HRS cells exhibit profound reprogramming of their transcriptional identity, characterized by near-complete loss of B-cell-specific gene expression and aberrant activation of key signaling pathways, most notably NF-κB. Constitutive NF-κB activation is driven by multiple mechanisms, including genetic lesions such as inactivating mutations in TNFAIP3, copy number gains of REL and MAP3K14, and microenvironmental signaling via CD30, CD40, and BCMA. In approximately 40% of cases, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection contributes to NF-κB activation through latent membrane protein 1 (LMP1), particularly in tumors with BCR-defective precursors.

Additional molecular aberrations include frequent mutations in SOCS-1, leading to sustained JAK/STAT5 signaling and promoting survival and proliferation of HRS cells. Transcriptomic analyses reveal that HRS cells share gene expression signatures with rare CD30+ B-cell subsets in germinal centers and extrafollicular regions, suggesting a cellular origin from these transitional B-cell populations. These CD30+ B cells exhibit MYC-driven proliferation and redifferentiation patterns that may be co-opted during lymphomagenesis. Furthermore, HRS cells display genomic instability and multinuclearity, potentially linked to downregulation of genes involved in cytokinesis and genomic integrity. Together, these findings illustrate a complex pathobiology in which B-cell lineage identity is subverted through combined genetic, epigenetic, and viral mechanisms to enable malignant transformation and immune evasion.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) exhibits a distinct bimodal age distribution, with the first peak occurring in young adults aged 15–35 years and a second, smaller peak in individuals over 55 years of age, as documented in large population-based studies ref [9]. This pattern is consistent across Western populations and is mirrored in histologic subtypes, with nodular sclerosis being the most common in adolescents and young adults, while mixed cellularity predominates in older patients and in developing countries ref [6]. Systemic B symptoms—fever, night sweats, and weight loss—are reported in approximately 40–50% of cases at diagnosis and are associated with advanced-stage disease and poorer prognosis ref [22]. The disease accounts for roughly 10–15% of all lymphomas in the United States, with an annual incidence of approximately 8,500 new cases ref [8]. Staging and response assessment are standardized using the Lugano classification, which integrates clinical evaluation, imaging (particularly PET/CT), and histopathology to guide risk-adapted therapy ref [10]. Notably, pediatric and adolescent patients demonstrate superior survival outcomes compared to adults, with 5-year HL-specific survival rates exceeding 95% versus 88% in adults, even after adjusting for stage and histology ref [9]. Geographic and racial disparities exist, with higher incidence in high-income countries and increased prevalence of mixed cellularity subtype in Hispanic and lower socioeconomic populations, potentially linked to Epstein-Barr virus exposure ref [22].

subsections.section_title: Treatment Strategies for Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Pediatric-Specific Treatment Paradigms and Late-Effect Mitigation
subsections.content:
Pediatric classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) treatment has evolved toward risk-adapted, response-guided strategies aimed at preserving long-term survival while minimizing therapy-related late effects. Dose-intensive, response-based chemotherapy regimens such as ABVE-PC and OEPA-COPDAC have replaced older, more toxic protocols, allowing for reduced cumulative doses of alkylating agents and anthracyclines without compromising cure rates ref [25]. The GPOH-HD-2002 study demonstrated that procarbazine-free regimens in boys (OEPA-COPDAC) achieve outcomes comparable to standard OPPA-COPP in girls, reducing gonadotoxic and leukemogenic risks ref [27]. Building on earlier trials like GPOH-HD 95, which showed feasibility of limiting radiotherapy to 20 Gy or omitting it entirely in complete responders, modern approaches now integrate PET-based response assessment to guide radiation omission ref [28]. The Childhood Hodgkin International Prognostic Score (CHIPS) enables early risk stratification at diagnosis, facilitating personalized therapy intensity ref [30]. Recent phase II trials incorporating brentuximab vedotin and rituximab with reduced chemotherapy cycles have achieved 100% complete response rates and 5-year event-free survival, with radiotherapy reserved for only 13% of patients ref [15]. Response-based omission of radiotherapy in intermediate- and high-risk pediatric cHL has been shown to maintain excellent progression-free survival (>95%) while eliminating long-term radiation-induced morbidities such as secondary malignancies and cardiovascular disease ref [9]. The NCCN Guidelines emphasize these principles, advocating for chemotherapy-only strategies in favorable responders and strict avoidance of radiotherapy in low-risk settings ref [26].

Biomarker-driven approaches are increasingly critical for identifying patients at highest risk of late effects, particularly secondary malignancies, which occur 10- to 175-fold more frequently in pediatric cHL survivors than in the general population ref [12]. Ongoing research focuses on substituting alkylating agents with targeted agents like brentuximab vedotin to reduce genotoxic burden, while preserving efficacy ref [15]. Future paradigms will integrate genomic profiling, early metabolic response, and longitudinal biomarker monitoring to further de-escalate therapy in low-risk subgroups and intensify only where necessary, ensuring that cure is achieved without compromising lifelong health ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Treatment Strategies for Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Immunotherapy and Targeted Agents in First-Line and Relapsed Settings
subsections.content:
Immunotherapy has revolutionized the treatment of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL), particularly through blockade of the PD-1 pathway, which is exploited by Reed-Sternberg cells to evade immune surveillance. The genetic amplification of 9p24.1, leading to increased expression of PD-L1 and PD-L2, provides a mechanistic rationale for the high efficacy of PD-1 inhibitors in cHL, as demonstrated in both relapsed/refractory and first-line settings ref [16]. Nivolumab and pembrolizumab have shown durable response rates exceeding 80% in heavily pretreated patients, with pembrolizumab demonstrating superior progression-free survival compared to brentuximab vedotin in the KEYNOTE-204 trial ref [33]. This advantage is further supported by improved health-related quality of life outcomes with pembrolizumab, including sustained global health status and delayed time to deterioration across multiple domains ref [37]. Building on these findings, pembrolizumab is now approved for use in pediatric and adolescent patients following autologous stem cell transplantation, offering a nonchemotherapeutic consolidation strategy ref [19].

Emerging targeted combinations are expanding the therapeutic horizon. The bispecific antibody AFM13, which engages CD16A on natural killer cells to target CD30-expressing tumor cells, has shown promising safety and preliminary efficacy when combined with pembrolizumab in relapsed/refractory cHL, suggesting synergistic activation of innate and adaptive immunity ref [7]. These advances, alongside the integration of PD-1 inhibitors into frontline regimens for high-risk patients, reflect a paradigm shift toward immune-based, risk-adapted strategies that reduce reliance on cytotoxic chemotherapy and mitigate long-term toxicities ref [18]. Ongoing trials are evaluating PD-1 blockade in combination with novel agents such as JAK inhibitors, leveraging the molecular link between 9p24.1 amplification and JAK2 signaling ref [16]. The evolving landscape underscores a move toward precision immunotherapy, where molecular profiling guides therapeutic selection across disease stages.

subsections.section_title: Treatment Strategies for Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Risk-Adapted and PET-Guided Strategies in Advanced-Stage Disease
subsections.content:
Risk-adapted, PET-guided strategies have transformed the management of advanced-stage classical Hodgkin lymphoma by enabling therapy intensification or de-escalation based on early metabolic response. The HD18 trial demonstrated that patients with a positive PET-2 scan after two cycles of eBEACOPP benefit from intensified therapy, while those with a negative PET-2 can be safely treated with fewer cycles, reducing toxicity without compromising efficacy ref [39]. Similarly, the AHL2011 trial established non-inferiority of switching from escalated BEACOPP to ABVD in PET-2-negative patients, supporting de-escalation as a viable strategy to mitigate long-term toxicities ref [40]. In contrast, the SWOG S0816 trial showed that PET-adapted escalation to eBEACOPP in PET-2-positive patients achieved a 5-year progression-free survival of 66%, underscoring the prognostic value of interim PET but also highlighting residual relapse risk ref [11]. The GITIL/FIL HD0607 trial further validated early intensification with escalated BEACOPP in ABVD-treated PET-2-positive patients, confirming improved progression-free survival with this approach ref [10]. Importantly, consolidation radiotherapy can be safely omitted in patients achieving complete metabolic response after ABVD, even with bulky disease, as shown in the HD0607 trial ref [9]. These findings collectively support a dynamic, response-driven paradigm that balances efficacy with toxicity reduction.

The integration of novel agents into PET-guided frameworks is emerging, with brentuximab vedotin (BV) now established as a backbone in first-line therapy for advanced disease. The ECHELON-1 trial demonstrated superior progression-free survival with BV combined with AVD (A+AVD) compared to ABVD, prompting re-evaluation of PET-guided strategies in this context ref [42]. Subsequent North American validation confirmed the safety and efficacy of A+AVD, reinforcing its role in risk-adapted regimens ref [43]. Ongoing trials are now exploring whether PET-2 response can further refine the use of BV-containing regimens, potentially allowing for even more precise de-escalation in early responders. The convergence of metabolic imaging and targeted therapy represents the next frontier in personalizing treatment for advanced Hodgkin lymphoma.

subsections.section_title: Treatment Strategies for Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Evolution of First-Line Chemotherapy and Radiotherapy in Early-Stage Disease
subsections.content:
The evolution of first-line therapy for early-stage classical Hodgkin lymphoma has shifted from radiation-only regimens to combined modality approaches, with a consistent emphasis on reducing long-term toxicity while preserving high cure rates. Early trials demonstrated that radiotherapy alone could achieve durable remissions in favorable disease, with low-dose extended-field radiotherapy (30 Gy) showing non-inferiority to higher doses (40 Gy) in terms of relapse-free and overall survival, establishing the feasibility of dose reduction ref [45]. Subsequent studies confirmed that involved-field radiotherapy (IFRT) could replace subtotal nodal irradiation without compromising efficacy, significantly lowering the risk of secondary malignancies and organ toxicity ref [46]. The integration of chemotherapy, particularly ABVD, further improved outcomes, leading to the standardization of 2–4 cycles of ABVD followed by reduced-dose IFRT (20–30 Gy) in both favorable and unfavorable subgroups ref [47]. The HD8 trial established that IFRT was equally effective and less toxic than extended-field radiotherapy after chemotherapy in unfavorable early-stage disease, reinforcing the paradigm shift toward targeted radiation ref [8]. The HD11 trial further refined this approach by demonstrating that dose-reduced IFRT (20 Gy) after intensified chemotherapy (e.g., escalated BEACOPP) maintained high efficacy in high-risk patients, enabling further de-escalation ref [11].

More recent evidence from the HD14 trial explored dose-intensified chemotherapy regimens, but confirmed that the primary driver of improved outcomes was not chemotherapy intensity per se, but rather the precision of radiation field definition and dose reduction ref [12]. Together, these landmark trials have redefined first-line management, moving away from broad-field, high-dose radiation toward risk-adapted, chemotherapy-sparing, and radiation-reduced strategies that prioritize long-term quality of life without sacrificing cure rates.

subsections.section_title: Treatment Strategies for Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.subsection_title: Salvage Therapy and Transplantation Strategies for Relapsed/Refractory Disease
subsections.content:
For patients with relapsed or refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma, high-dose chemotherapy followed by autologous hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (ASCT) remains the standard salvage approach for those achieving chemosensitivity. Outcomes have significantly improved over the past two decades, particularly with optimized conditioning regimens and pre-transplant immunotherapy. A 15-year analysis demonstrated that vorinostat/gemcitabine/busulfan/melphalan (vorinostat/GemBuMel) yielded superior 5-year progression-free and overall survival compared to BEAM or BuMel, with pre-ASCT brentuximab vedotin (BV) and PET-negativity emerging as strong favorable predictors ref [52]. In pediatric populations, CBV conditioning with peripheral blood stem cells has shown acceptable toxicity and 3-year event-free survival of 66% in transplanted patients, though early relapse (<12 months) remains a poor prognostic factor ref [53]. Initial response to salvage chemotherapy is critically predictive; inadequate response correlates with a 5-year overall survival of only 17.9% versus 97.2% in responders, underscoring the need for early transition to novel agents ref [56].

Prognostic models incorporating factors such as B symptoms, extranodal involvement, and duration of first remission have been validated to stratify risk, with patients harboring three adverse features exhibiting <10% event-free survival ref [12]. In children, relapse within 6 months of initial therapy and involvement of irradiated fields are associated with inferior outcomes ref [9]. For patients failing ASCT or with primary refractory disease, allogeneic transplantation offers a potentially curative option, particularly in young, fit individuals, leveraging graft-versus-lymphoma effects ref [15]. The integration of brentuximab vedotin and immune checkpoint inhibitors into pre- and post-transplant strategies is reshaping the salvage landscape, enabling more patients to achieve transplant eligibility and improving durability of response.

subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Toxicity and Novel Targeted Approaches
subsections.content:
Therapeutic toxicity in classical Hodgkin lymphoma remains a significant concern, particularly with conventional chemoradiotherapy regimens that predispose patients to long-term organ damage, secondary malignancies, and cardiovascular complications. To mitigate these effects, novel targeted approaches have emerged, focusing on disrupting key oncogenic pathways while sparing normal tissues. The dual PI3Kδ/γ inhibitor RP6530 exemplifies this shift, demonstrating potent activity against both Hodgkin/Reed–Sternberg cells and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment by repolarizing tumor-associated macrophages from M2 to M1 phenotypes and inhibiting tumor glycolysis via pyruvate kinase M2 downregulation ref [57]. Similarly, agents targeting the CD30 pathway, such as brentuximab vedotin, have reduced reliance on alkylating agents and anthracyclines, lowering acute and late toxicities ref [7]. Emerging inhibitors of JAK/STAT and NF-κB signaling, driven by recurrent genetic alterations in Hodgkin lymphoma, offer additional precision options ref [36]. Furthermore, immune checkpoint blockade with pembrolizumab has shown durable responses in relapsed/refractory disease with a more favorable toxicity profile compared to salvage chemotherapy ref [40]. These targeted strategies collectively represent a paradigm shift toward reducing cumulative toxicity while enhancing efficacy.

Ongoing clinical trials are evaluating combinations of PI3K inhibitors with PD-1 blockade to amplify antitumor immunity and overcome resistance mechanisms, with early data suggesting synergistic effects in modulating the tumor microenvironment ref [57]. The integration of biomarker-driven patient selection—such as 9p24.1 amplification status—further refines therapeutic precision and minimizes unnecessary exposure to toxic agents ref [28]. As these approaches mature, they hold promise for de-escalating traditional cytotoxic regimens without compromising survival outcomes.

subsections.subsection_title: Long-Term Surveillance and Late Effects of Treatment
subsections.content:
Survivors of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) face a significant burden of late effects stemming from curative therapies, including chemotherapy and radiotherapy. These include secondary malignancies, cardiovascular disease, pulmonary dysfunction, endocrine disorders, and infertility, with risks persisting for decades after treatment. The landmark study by Ng and van Leeuwen provides a comprehensive framework for long-term surveillance, emphasizing risk-stratified follow-up based on treatment exposure, age at diagnosis, and genetic predisposition ref [58]. Radiation-induced solid tumors, particularly breast and thyroid cancers, are markedly elevated in patients treated with mediastinal irradiation, especially when administered during adolescence. Anthracycline-based regimens contribute to cardiomyopathy, while bleomycin exposure is linked to pulmonary fibrosis, necessitating periodic pulmonary function testing. Endocrine sequelae, such as hypothyroidism and premature ovarian insufficiency, require routine hormonal monitoring. Recent guidelines advocate for lifelong surveillance protocols, integrating imaging, biomarkers, and patient-reported outcomes to detect complications early.

Emerging evidence underscores the importance of survivorship care plans tailored to individual risk profiles, with multidisciplinary teams playing a pivotal role in coordinating long-term care. Studies have demonstrated that adherence to surveillance guidelines improves early detection and survival from secondary cancers, yet implementation remains suboptimal in many settings. Ongoing research continues to refine risk prediction models by incorporating genomic and treatment-response biomarkers, aiming to balance cure with quality of life in the modern era of de-escalated therapy.

subsections.subsection_title: Role of Heat-Shock Proteins in Treatment Resistance and Survival
subsections.content:
Heat-shock proteins (HSPs) play a pivotal role in the pathobiology of classical Hodgkin lymphoma by promoting tumor cell survival, mitigating proteotoxic stress, and conferring resistance to conventional therapies. HSP70, HSP90, and HSP27 are overexpressed in Reed-Sternberg cells, where they stabilize oncogenic signaling molecules, inhibit apoptosis, and facilitate DNA repair mechanisms under chemotherapy-induced stress. Notably, HSP90 supports the stability of key survival pathways such as NF-κB and JAK/STAT, both of which are constitutively activated in Hodgkin lymphoma, thereby contributing to treatment evasion. Ref [1] provides a comprehensive overview of HSP multitargeting in hematological malignancies, highlighting their central role in therapeutic resistance and their potential as biomarkers of poor prognosis. Emerging evidence suggests that HSP110 may modulate immune evasion by influencing antigen presentation, further linking chaperone activity to the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment characteristic of Hodgkin lymphoma.

Preclinical studies have demonstrated that pharmacological inhibition of HSP90 with agents such as geldanamycin derivatives or newer-generation inhibitors like ganetespib can sensitize Hodgkin lymphoma cell lines to doxorubicin and brentuximab vedotin, suggesting synergistic therapeutic potential. Moreover, HSP27 knockdown has been shown to enhance caspase activation and reduce clonogenic survival in vitro, reinforcing its role as a cytoprotective factor. While clinical trials targeting HSPs in Hodgkin lymphoma remain limited, the mechanistic rationale is strong, particularly in relapsed/refractory settings where conventional therapies fail. Future strategies may combine HSP inhibitors with immune checkpoint blockade, leveraging the dual impact of HSPs on both intrinsic survival pathways and immune modulation.

Figure 2 illustrates the molecular and microenvironmental drivers of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL), highlighting the central role of Reed-Sternberg (RS) cells and their interactions with the tumor microenvironment. RS cells, derived from germinal center B-cells, exhibit defective immunoglobulin transcription despite functional gene rearrangements, enabling immune evasion and survival ref [20]. Genetic alterations such as 9p24.1 amplification lead to increased PD-L1/PD-L2 expression, facilitating immune checkpoint evasion ref [30]. Concurrently, mutations in SOCS-1 result in constitutive JAK/STAT signaling, promoting proliferation and cytokine production ref [37]. The tumor microenvironment is enriched with regulatory T cells, macrophages, and fibroblasts, which secrete survival factors such as IL-13 and CD30L, further supporting RS cell persistence ref [27]. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection, present in a subset of cHL cases, contributes to pathogenesis through LMP1-mediated NF-κB activation and immune modulation ref [16]. Additionally, dysregulation of NF-κB pathways, often via mutations in TNFAIP3 or NFKBIE, sustains anti-apoptotic signaling ref [38]. These interconnected mechanisms underscore the therapeutic rationale for targeting both RS cells and their supportive niche.

Recent preclinical studies have demonstrated the efficacy of dual PI3Kδ/γ inhibition in disrupting RS cell survival signals and reprogramming the immunosuppressive microenvironment ref [59]. Furthermore, the identification of CD30+ B cells as a potential precursor population provides new insights into the cellular origin of RS cells ref [27]. Together, these findings support the development of combination therapies targeting intrinsic oncogenic pathways and extrinsic immune evasion mechanisms.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is characterized by a sparse population of malignant Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells embedded within a complex, immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). The TME is dominated by T regulatory cells, macrophages, and fibroblasts, which are co-opted by HRS cells through cytokine and chemokine signaling to promote immune evasion and tumor survival. Notably, HRS cells frequently exhibit constitutive activation of the NF-κB pathway, which drives the expression of pro-survival genes and immune modulators such as PD-L1 and CD30 ref [57]. Additionally, genetic alterations at 9p24.1, including amplification and copy number gains, lead to increased expression of PD-L1 and PD-L2, enhancing immune checkpoint evasion ref [19]. The JAK-STAT pathway is further activated via SOCS-1 mutations, which impair negative regulation and result in sustained STAT phosphorylation ref [18]. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection in a subset of cHL cases contributes to this dysregulation through LMP1-mediated NF-κB and JAK/STAT activation ref [11]. Recent studies highlight the role of PI3Kδ/γ signaling in sustaining HRS cell viability and modulating the TME, with dual inhibitors showing preclinical efficacy ref [13]. The interplay between HRS cells and the TME also involves CD30 signaling, which promotes survival and proliferation, and is exploited therapeutically by brentuximab vedotin ref [35].

Emerging evidence suggests that the TME in cHL is not merely a passive bystander but an active participant in disease progression and therapy resistance. Targeting both HRS cells and their supportive stroma—through combinations of checkpoint inhibitors, kinase inhibitors, and immunomodulators—represents a promising frontier in cHL treatment ref [13]. The success of PD-1 blockade in relapsed/refractory cHL underscores the centrality of immune evasion mechanisms, while ongoing trials explore novel agents targeting the PI3K, JAK, and NF-κB axes to overcome resistance ref [19][5][6].
